1: This is the executive briefing for Book 08 of the Federal Modernization Workbook: D N S, DHCP and IP address management.
It's for the C I O, the see-so, the network and infrastructure lead, and sponsors.
Almost every connection starts with a D N S query, and the answer now decides far more than an address.
Most agencies still run D N S across several platforms that share nothing, so the same name gets different answers, and the failures look like something else.
The fix is one authoritative policy plane, with named owners.
I'll take four questions: why, what, who and how.
Each decision slide names the decision, its owner and when it's needed.
Let's start with what D N S now does.
2: D N S was built to turn names into numbers, in a world where inside and outside were separated by a wire.
Today the answer to a D N S query decides whether cloud traffic stays private, which SaaS front door a user reaches, whether a malicious domain is blocked, and whether a certificate check succeeds.
It's also the name a Zero Trust policy is written against.
nist's 2026 guide says it plainly: D N S is now a security control, not just a service.
So the first point for this room is that governing D N S is a security and architecture job, not an operations chore.
Next, what happens when it isn't governed.
3: Nobody chooses to run D N S in five places.
Each cloud ships its own D N S service, and none of them shares state with Active Directory or with each other.
So the same name drifts into different answers depending on where the query starts.
That's split-brain, and it fails quietly: the name still resolves, just to the wrong place, and it shows up as a certificate error or an access denial.
Runbooks can't keep five systems in step, and your real security posture is the weakest resolver a client can reach.
So the decision for the sponsor and C I O: authorize one authoritative policy plane, before the next migration wave.
4: M twenty-two oh-nine says agencies must encrypt D N S wherever it's technically supported, and point devices at agency-designated resolvers, not whatever they discover.
And sis-uh's Protective D N S is mandatory for all outbound resolution.
The two fit together: encrypt, but end at your own resolvers, with Protective D N S upstream.
Where it breaks is the device.
Encrypted D N S that rides the ordinary web port can't be seen by the network, so it has to be governed through device and browser policy.
The decision belongs to the see-so: designate the resolvers and the allowed transports, now.
An exception with no end date goes to the authorizing official.
Next, the rest of the floor.
5: O M B's May 2026 memo, M-26-14, replaced the old logging tiers.
It doesn't name D N S at all; it sets a baseline, logs searchable for six months and kept for a year, and leaves the sources to each agency's logging plan.
That plan is due by November 18, a date we computed from sis-uh's publication.
D N S query logs tell you which address asked for a bad domain; DHCP lease logs tell you which device that was.
So the see-so puts both in the plan.
DNSSEC and the IPv6 targets are older requirements, and the IPv6 dates have passed.
Now, what has to change, starting with Active Directory.
6: For twenty years Active Directory quietly ran your D N S. Domain controllers host the zones and publish the records that let machines find them.
None of that moves to Entra ID.
Entra ID hosts no zones at all, and some systems will keep needing domain controllers for a while.
Here's the trap: once a domain controller is gone, the records it kept can't be recovered from it.
So leaving A D D N S is an inventory problem before it's a migration problem.
The decision: the D N S and D D I team owns the inventory, A D administrators do the work, and it's reconciled before the first domain controller goes.
Next, how queries slip past your controls.
7: Every control you buy assumes the query reaches it.
Three ordinary things decide whether it does, and none of them raises an alarm.
A branch network edge can redirect D N S to a resolver outside your control.
A device or browser can send encrypted D N S straight to a public service.
And a rogue DHCP server can hand a whole subnet an attacker's resolver in one step.
So the decision splits deciding from doing.
The D N S and D D I team decides that every edge points only at agency resolvers; network engineering configures it; and the see-so owns rogue DHCP detection.
Do it as authority moves, then check before every change.
8: A certificate can be valid and unrevoked and still fail, because every check that makes it trustworthy starts with a D N S lookup.
If the revocation names live only in Active Directory D N S, a cloud workload can't reach them, and the ticket gets opened as a certificate problem.
The same goes for sign-in endpoints and wildcard names.
The program's position: sign your external zones always, validate on resolvers you control, and sign internal zones only where it's required.
And moving a zone somewhere it can't be signed is a risk acceptance, so the authorizing official decides it.
9: Names and addresses are the same problem.
Every cloud has its own address manager, and left alone each one hands out address space on its own.
You find the overlap when two networks are joined, or an auditor finds space nobody recorded.
So the enterprise eye-pam is the authority for address blocks.
Some platforms integrate natively; others need you to reserve first, mirror, and reconcile.
Either way it becomes the address layer of the asset inventory Zero Trust depends on.
The decision: the D N S and D D I team owns the address plan, and every new cloud network is reserved in eye-pam before it's created.
10: The architecture is simple to draw.
Branch edge, then an agency resolver, then the policy plane, then each cloud's private zones, with internet queries leaving through Protective D N S.
The risk sits in five settings: where the edge points, which resolver goes first, where cloud forwarding rules live, the A D D N S inventory, and whether revocation names resolve from everywhere.
Each fails silently, so each needs a check in the live configuration, not the design.
The book's ask is specific: the D N S and D D I team settles all five within ninety days of authorizing the plane, and reports the remaining risk to the authorizing official.
11: The platform decision is really a decision about the source of truth.
One plane holds the zones, the forwarding rules, the address data and the security policy, and the cloud D N S services consume it.
There are three models: a SaaS policy plane, D D I the agency runs itself, or cloud-native services managed as code.
Each has a trade-off, and a small single-cloud agency may need only the last.
Remember that fed-ramp certifies a service, not your system, and Moderate doesn't cover High.
So the sponsor and C I O choose on evidence from your own estate, and the authorizing official authorizes any cloud-delivered plane.
12: In an Active Directory estate, nobody wrote down who owned D N S, because A D did it for you.
One admin group controlled every zone, and the domain controller team decided by default.
A single policy plane concentrates that power: one team can now break resolution for every user and every cloud at once.
So owners have to be named on purpose, one decider per decision, or the cloud, network and directory teams each own a piece by accident.
Two decisions before the transition starts.
The sponsor and C I O give the decision rights to a named group.
And A D administrators strip the D N S admin group down to domain administrators.
13: Here's the matrix in one view.
The sponsor and C I O decide the platform and when the old services retire.
The see-so decides encryption, DNSSEC and logging.
The D N S and D D I team decides the namespace, the edge target, the forwarding and the address plan.
Network engineering and A D administrators do much of the work, but don't decide it.
Why does the authorizing official appear twice?
Because many D N S changes are risk decisions in disguise.
Pointing an edge at a public resolver quietly turns off Protective D N S.
So every standing exception goes to the authorizing official, with an owner and a review date.
14: Most D N S changes don't need a change board.
Treat them all alike and you get either a six-week wait for a simple record, or no control at all.
So the program uses three classes.
Standard changes inside a delegated namespace are approved in advance.
Records written by a policy need no approval each time, but the policy itself does.
And high-impact changes, like zones, forwarding and wildcards, go to the board.
One more point: the account the plane uses to write into each cloud is the most powerful identity in the design, so guard it.
The D N S and D D I team adopts the classes before namespaces are delegated.
15: The migration runs in six phases: inventory, coexist, move authority, bring in the clouds, retire A D D N S and DHCP, then harden and prove it.
Name resolution has to keep working while authority moves, so every move runs the same small loop.
The old system keeps answering until the new one is proven from every location, and a failed check just switches back.
The program has planning estimates, from a day or two up to a few weeks, but they're estimates, not commitments.
The decision: the D N S and D D I team closes each phase on its evidence, never on a calendar date.
Next, the step you can't undo.
16: This is where D N S meets the identity program.
While any domain controller remains, it needs D N S that accepts its registrations, so those records are the last thing to move.
Retiring A D D N S is the one step you can't cheaply undo, so it's gated, not scheduled.

Five gates, all program design: the inventory reconciles; the critical records resolve everywhere for thirty days; ninety days of parallel running; failover actually tested; and no traffic left on the old servers.
Get it wrong and you get forest-wide sign-in failures.
So the sponsor and C I O set the date only after every gate passes, with the records officer involved.
17: One plane only helps if divisions can still run their own networks through it, and every change leaves a trace.
So divisions get scoped control, and every change, by a person or a script, goes through one interface and one audit trail.
The logs feed security operations, the inventory and the authorization package.
And measure one thing first: resolution-path consistency, meaning the same name gets the intended answer from every location.
Baseline it now, set a target, and report it.
The book doesn't say who reports, so in our model it's the D N S and D D I team, reporting to the authorizing official.
18: Commercial D D I licensing isn't published, so get quotes from every candidate on the same assumptions.
The cloud pieces do have public prices, and every model uses them.

One region's cloud resolver hub runs about three hundred and sixty dollars a month before zones and queries, and the book corrects earlier guidance that got the pricing backwards, so re-check any budget built on it.
Some risk remains after the plane is in: sync lag, a management outage that blocks changes, encrypted D N S bypass, and the limits of a Moderate authorization.
The sponsor and C I O handle this before selection, and record the residual risk.
19: The sponsor and C I O authorize one policy plane, choose the platform on evidence, name the decision rights, and retire A D D N S only through the gates.

The see-so designates the encrypted resolvers now, puts D N S and DHCP logs in the logging plan by November 18, and sets signing and validation, with standing exceptions going to the authorizing official.

The D N S and D D I team reconciles the A D inventory before any domain controller goes, aims every edge at agency resolvers, makes eye-pam the address authority, and settles the five decisions within ninety days.
Govern the name layer before the last domain controller goes.
Book 08 has the detail, every claim footnoted.
